# ARTICLE INFO --- *Article history:* Received 7 January 2020 Received in revised form 29 April 2020 Accepted 2 May 2020 Available online 16 May 2020 --- *Keywords:* Biomass Cellulose Natural deep eutectic solvents Conversion Total reducing sugars

ABSTRACT Lignocellulosic biomass contains about 45% cellulose. The total reducing sugars (TRS) obtained from lignocellu-losic materials is beneficial to the sustainable development. Natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESS) provide an attractive alternative for the "green" conversion of cellulose. In this work, series of amino acids based NADESS with FeCl36H2O as ligands catalyst were synthesized and characterized by in situ IR, FT-IR, 1H NMR and TG-DTA. NADESS showed great thermal stability. The efficient hydrolysis performance of cellulose in NADESs was inves-tigated under mild conditions. The influencing factors such as the type of NADESS, reaction temperature, reaction time, and FeCl36H2O addition on the TRS yield were studied. The optimized process conditions for hydrolyzing cellulose in L-Proline/ Ethylene glycol/FeCl36H2O were molar ratio 1: 2: 1, reaction time 120 min and tempera-ture 120 °C. The yield of total reducing sugar was 66.7%. The conversion mechanism was also investigated. © 2020 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

# 1. Introduction Concerns about fossil carbon depletion and global climate change have led to an increasing focus on biomass conversion to sustainably supply liquid fuels and valuable chemicals. Therefore, the search for renewable energy to replace fossil fuels has become a top priority. According to the forecast made by the US Department of Energy, the amount of liquid fuels consumed in the US from biofuels should increase 200% due to the Federal Renewable Fuels Standard, which requires 36 billion gallons of renewable fuel to be blended into transportation fuels by 2022 [1]. Recently, biomass conversion has become a research hotspot of many scholars at home and abroad, and different methods have been developed to convert biomass into fuels, chemicals and materials [2–5].

Biomass resources are the only renewable organic carbon resources in nature. Lignocellulose is the most abundant green renewable re-source and the main structural form of plants [6-9]. Lignocellulose con-sists of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin, with an annual production of about 170 billion tons, of which about 45% is cellulose [10-12]. Cellulose is the most prolific component of lignocellulose, which is a linear poly-mer compound obtained by linking D-glucopyranose to 1,4-β glycoside

The cellulose molecule contains a large amount of hydroxyl groups inside, and since hydrogen bonds are easily generated between the hydroxyl group and the hydroxyl group, a large number of hydrogen bonds exist inside and between the cellulose molecules, forming a strong hydrogen bond network structure [15–17]. Therefore, cellulose is extremely difficult to dissolve in water or other conventional organic solvents, which seriously affects the contact between the catalyst and cellulose molecules and becomes the biggest obstacle to cellulose conversion.

In the past few decades, research on the conversion of cellulose has developed rapidly. Conversion of cellulose into various value-added chemicals and fuels, such as various alcohols [18], gluconic acid [19], 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) [20], lactic acid [21], pentanoic acid esters [22], 2,5-dimethylfuran [23], and levulinic acid [24], has been studied extensively in recent years. The catalytic oxidation of cellulose to total reducing sugars (TRS) is one of the most promising pathways. TRS is used as a fine chemical product, and it is widely used in the pharmaceutical, food and industrial industries.

In recent decades, ionic liquids (ILs) have been thought of as suitable solvents instead of sulfuric acid for conversion owing to their unique properties, including negligible vapor pressure, high thermal stability, and good solvent power for different kinds of substances [25]. In 2018, Saliha Saher [26] synthesized a pyridinium-based ionic liquid [C4C₁Py] [Cl], which was used for the dissolution of cellulose, with a solubility of up to 28% at 110 °C, and continued in the presence of the metal salt

As an attractive alternative to ILs and conventional organic solvents, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged and have evolved signifi- cantly [27]. DESs are usually binary mixtures of hydrogen bond accep- tors (HBA) and hydrogen bond donors (HBD). At a certain molar ratio, the freezing point is lower than the melting point of the pure compound constituting DESs [28]. DESs have similar solvent properties to ILs such as the low-cost, good renewability and low toxicity [29]. Moreover, they are easy to prepare under mild conditions.

In recent works, there are many DESs which have been prepared for cellulose conversion. In 2012, Francisco et al. [30]. obtained a variety of DES solvent systems using representative natural substances commonly found in nature such as amino acids, choline chloride, niacin, malic acid and lactic acid. It was found that most DES have weak cellulose conver- sion ability, and DES composed of proline and malic acid can also con- vert a certain amount of cellulose. In 2015, Procentese [31] synthesized glycerol/choline chloride (Gly/ChCl), urea/choline chloride (Urea/ChCl) and imidazole/choline chloride (Im/ChCl) DESs for corn core conversion. In this process, it was found that the DES promotes the saccharification conversion process by removing lignin and reduc- ing the crystallinity of the cellulose, and a total of 41 g of fermentable sugar (27 g of glucose and 14 g of xylose) can be recovered from 100 g of corn cob, accounting for 76% of the initial available reducing sugar. In 2016, Wahlstrom et al. [32] synthesized three choline chlo- rides: boric acid (5:2 M ratio), choline chloride: glycerol (molar ratio 1:1), and betaine: glycerol (molar ratio 1:1). The composition of the DES converted the wheat straw, and the stability of the wheat straw to TRS, and the yield after the residue hydrolysis were 33.0%, 20.0% and 19.0%, respectively. Overall, the conversion of cellulose in DESs is not ideal. Therefore, it is important to find efficient DESs with high con- version ability and selectivity to biomass.

As a kind of Lewis acid, Iron (III) chloride hexahydrate (FeCl36H2O) is widely used as catalyst in chemical reactions such as esterification, condensation, etherification and oxidation. It has the advantages of high catalytic activity, reusability and low price [33]. FeCl36H2O catalyzed hydrolysis reaction conditions are mild, less corrosion to equipment, simple operation, short reaction cycle, low cost, and environmental protection.

In this research, it was devoted to the synthesis of a novel series of amino acid based natural deep eutectic solvents (NADES) with FeCl36- H2O as ligands catalyst, and utilized to convert cellulose into the total re- ducing sugar. The physical properties of NADESs include freezing point, solvation parameters, pH, thermal stability and synthesis processes were investigated. The chemical properties of the NADESs such as ¹H NMR and FT-IR were also measured. The effects of different external fac- tors, such as different sorts of NADESs, temperature, time and FeCl36- H2O addition on cellulose conversion were studied. The conversion mechanism was also developed.

## 2. Experiments ### 2.1. Materials The cellulose was cotton linter pulp with a polymerization degree of 575.6 (Helon, China). The cotton linter pulp was cut into small pieces. After being dried at 100 °C for 12 h, the cellulose was prepared and used in the present study. N₂ (99.99%) was obtained from Beijing Haipu Gases Co., Ltd., Beijing, China. L-Proline, L-Lysine and L-Glutamic acid (99%) were purchased from Huayang Chemical Co., Ltd., Hebei, China. Iron(III) chloride hexahydrate (99%), Methanesulfonic acid (MSA) and p-Toluenesulfonic acid (TsOH) were obtained from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. Ethylene glycol and Glycerol (99%) was obtained from Tianjin Yongda Reagent Co., Ltd., Tianjin,
China. All chemical reagents used in this work were of analytical grade purity and were used directly.

2.2. Synthesis of NADESS A series of natural deep eutectic solvents were synthesized accord-ing to the previously methods [34]. The amino acids (L-Proline, L-Lysine, L-Glutamic acid, etc.) were used as hydrogen bond acceptors, ethylene glycol, _p_-toluenesulfonic acid, Methanesulfonic acid, etc. were used as hydrogen bond donors, and FeCl₃·6H₂O as ligands were added to a 100 mL round bottom three-necked flask at a certain ratio. The mixture was then heated at a heating rate of 5 °C·h⁻¹ from room temperature to 100 °C under magnetic stirring. The container was also protected with nitrogen until a uniform, stable liquid formed. The sample was then placed in a forced air oven at 60 °C for 24 h, and the products were ob-tained (Fig. 1).

2.3. Conversion of cellulose in NADESs 5 g of prepared NADESs was added to a 100 mL round bottom flask, and then heated at a heating rate of 5 °C·h⁻¹ from room temperature to 140 °C under magnetic stirring. Then 1 g cellulose was added to the flask and allowed to react for 2 h at a set temperature from 90 °C to 140 °C. The reaction was terminated immediately by placing in an ice water bath.

The cellulose conversion rate is calculated by measuring the change in mass before and after the reaction. After the reaction, the mixed solution was rapidly cooled, centrifuged and filtered. Ethanol was added to the solid residue as back extractant of cellulose. The insoluble cellulose solids were dried and weighed to calculate the conversion of cellulose [35].

Firstly, the unreacted cellulose solid was filtered when the reaction stopped. Then, the upper solution was precipitated with ethanol at a volume fraction of 80% (volume ratio of solution to ethanol was 1:4) [36-40]. After the so- lution stood for 4 h, and filtered the insoluble crude reducing sugars, and rotary evaporated the ethanol, NADESs was regenerated for the recycling. ## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Synthesis of natural deep eutectic solvents In the synthesis of NADESSs, the freezing point ($T_f$) was used to represent the eutectic of the mixture, indicating an interaction occurred between the mixtures to form a new liquid material [41-43]. The $T_f$ of L-Pro/EG, L-Lys/ EG, L-Pro/TsOH, L-Glu/Gly and L-Pro/MSA under optimized ratio were 24.6 °C (1: 2) and 26.4 °C (1:6) 29.5 °C (2: 1), 32.8 °C (1: 8) and 38.5 °C (1:2), respectively (Figs. ## 3.2. Properties of NADESs ### 3.2.1. Thermostability Thermal stability is a significant parameter related to cellulose conversion in NADESs. The thermodynamic properties of the synthesized NADESs were analyzed by DTG-TGA analysis (Fig. 2). The temperatures at different ratios of mass loss ($T_{10\%}$ and $T_{50\%}$) and the temperature of the maximum loss mass rate ($T_{\text{max}}$) were listed in Table 2 [45]. As can be seen from the figure, the weight loss of L-Pro/EG, L-Lys/EG, L-Pro/TsOH, L-Glu/Gly and L-Pro/MSA is 10% at 138.9 °C, 131.2 °C, 258 °C, 201.4 °C and 289 °C, respectively. It indicates that the prepared NADESs have good thermal stability to meet the hydrolysis of cellulose.

The synthesis process of the NADESs was monitored with FT-IR and in situ IR spectroscopy, respectively (Fig. 3(a-d)). In Fig. 3(a), the peak at a wavelength of 1621 cm⁻¹ denotes the N-H stretching vibration of the L-Proline. The characteristic peak 3355 cm⁻¹ is attributed to the -OH group in ethylene glycol. Comparing with the spectra of raw materials (L-Proline and ethylene glycol), the redshifts and increased peak breadth occur. The C-O stretching characteristic peak appears at 1039 cm⁻¹ for pure ethylene glycol, and it shifts to 1041 cm⁻¹ in the forming of NADESs between L-Proline and ethylene glycol. In the fingerprint region, some changes also occur alongside. All the changes in the spectrum demonstrate that L-Proline and ethylene glycol are interconnected through hydrogen bonds. The FT-IR results of other NADESs are referred to Figs. S6-S9.

The pH reflects the acidity of the solution, and it directly affects the conversion of cellulose. As shown in Fig. 6, the pH of NADESS was about 4-5 in the absence of FeCl3 · 6H2O, and it showed weak acidity. However, the acidity of the system increased to -1.8- -1.1 when FeCl3 · 6H2O was added. L-Lys/EG/FeCl3 · 6H2O was the most acidic sol- vent, but the yield of TRS was not the highest. It was possible that higher acidity would enhance certain side reactions, such as dehydration of glucose to 5-hydroxymethylfurfural. The acidity of L-Pro/EG/ FeCl3 · 6H2O was weaker than that of L-Lys/EG/FeCl3 · 6H2O, but the yield of TRS was the highest among these five systems. It could be con- cluded that proper acidity was favorable for increasing the TRS yield.

3.2.3. Solvation properties The Kamlet-Taft solvation model is often used to study the biomass conversion in liquid liquids or DESs. Solvation parameters include hydrogen bond acidity (α), hydrogen bond basicity (β), and polarizable effect (π*). The dipolar/polarizability is used to describe the non-specific part of the interaction between the solvent and the solute Van der Waals, such as dispersion, induction, and electrostatic interactions. Hydrogen bond basicity characterizes a compound's ability to give an electron pair as a hydrogen bond donor, and hydrogen bond acidic alpha indicates the compound's ability to accept an electron pair as a hydrogen bond acceptor.

As shown in Table 3, L-Pro/EG NADESs differed greatly from the other four types of NADESs in solvation properties, which had higher α values (1.58), lower β values (0.53), smaller π* (0.73), and E_T (30) (68.27 kcal mol⁻¹). These solvation parameters insured that the hydrogen-bond interaction between L-Pro and EG was stronger than others. Besides, the L-Pro/EG NADESS solution had weaker polarizability and stronger polarity. It indicated that it would have a better ability to bind electrons, which was beneficial for the formation of hydrogen bonds between NADESs and cellulose, thereby promoting the conver-sion of cellulose.

3.3.2. Effect of temperature on cellulose conversion As shown in Fig. 8, the effect of different reaction temperature on cellulose conversion and reducing sugar yield was investigated in the L-Proline/ethylene glycol/FeCl36H2O system. It could be seen that the conversion rate of cellulose and the yield of TRS increased firstly and then decreased as the reaction increasing temperature. When the reaction temperature was 90 °C, the yield of TRS was 25.3%. Continuously increasing the reaction temperature could promote a significant increase in the yield of TRS, and the yield of TRS reached the maximum of 66.7% when the temperature was 120 °C. During the hydrolysis, the increasing temperature can enhance the ionization of NADESS, so the chemical interaction between NADESs and the hydrogen and oxygen on the hydroxyl groups of the cellulose molecules is promoted, and the conversion of cellulose is significantly improved. However, higher temperature above 120 °C would lead to the degradation or repolymerization of carbohydrates, and the yield of reducing sugar decreased to some extent correspondingly. The main degraded products and their compositions were compared (Tables S1, S2). The main carbohydrate products were glucose (43.57%, relative peak area), fructose (4.93%), and cellobiose (10.95%) at 120 °C. The glucose-degraded products of pyruvaldehyde and gluconic acid were also detected, and the compositions were relatively much low. There was still a large unknown peak in the spectrum, and it might be due to the limitations of the analytical column and chromatographic conditions, making it impossible to analyze all the components in the liquid product. However, the products in hydrolysates changed greatly with the increasing of temperature 140 °C. About 29.29% of glucose was converted to gluconic

acid under the strong oxidative power of FeCl₃ [46–49]. The yield of pyruvaldehyde also increased from 2.46% to 5.42%. Besides, polar organic products such as ketones, aldehydes and acids were detected by GC-MS. The 5-HMF and furfural accounted for the most part of hydrolysis products. With the increasing temperature, they were further degraded to formic acid and levulinic acid.

However, the surface of residual cellulose solid is completely changed. The strip-like crystal cellulose become rough and disordered, and even irregular holes ap- peared, indicating the crystalline structure is converted to amorphous carbon (Fig. S15b). To compare the FTIR results of original cellulose and residual cellulose, there is no new peak occurred, but only slight blue shifts and enhanced peak strength. It demonstrates that the resi- dues of cellulose hydrolysis are still dominated by cellulose (Fig. S16). In Fig. S17, the first decomposition temperatures of the two materials are 276.3 °C and 292.5 °C, respectively. The maximum weightlessness temperatures are 337.3 °C and 370.1 °C, respectively. The results meant that the thermodynamic stability of residual solid is poor than that of the original cellulose. It also can be found that the amount of res- idue (about 30%) generated after thermal cracking of the residue is sig- nificantly higher than that of pure cellulose (less than 17%), it might be due to the some coke and ash generated during the cellulose hydrolysis.

On the basis of experimental results and the previous literature [33], the possible reaction mechanism was proposed as Scheme 1. Firstly, raw materials L-Proline, EG, and the ligands catalyst of FeCl36H2O reacted with each other to form O---HN and O---H---FeCl36H2O, and the L- Pro/EG/FeCl36H2O system was synthesized successfully. Secondly, 1,4- β glycoside bonds in cellulose were broken greenly under the strong acidity of L-Pro/EG/FeCl36H2O. Cellulose could be transformed into total reducing sugars in the L-Pro/EG/FeCl36H2O system.

3.3.5. Regeneration of NADESs In the regeneration of NADESs, the unreacted cellulose solid and the residual reducing sugars are all need to be removed. For the unreacted cellulose solid, it could be filtered when the reaction stopped. For the most part of NADESs, the sugar is insoluble in ethanol as studied [36–40], so the reducing sugars could be precipitated from ethylene glycol and glycerol with ethanol. Because the structure of the reducing sugars are similar to ethylene glycol and glycerol, the reducing sugars would react with amino acids (L-Proline) owing to the hydrogen bond

between the two materials. The residual reducing sugars also need pu- rity from the amino acids (L-Proline). To solve this problem, the differ- ent polarity of L-Proline and the reducing sugars can be used [51]. L- Proline is a kind of non-polar amino acid, and the reducing sugars are polar substance. Therefore, the low-polarity butanone was introduced to "extract" L-Proline from the reducing sugars, and the high-purified NADES and catalyst mixture were regenerated. The reusability of NADESs was carried out, and the results showed that the TRS yield was 59.5% after eight recycles, which was slight decreased than that of the first run (66.7%) (Fig. S15). The NADESs has good catalytic stability in the hydrolysis of cellulose to TRS.

## 4. Conclusions In this work, a novel series of NADESS with FeCl36H2O as ligands catalyst were synthesized and applied in catalytic conversion of cellulose to TRS, which had great thermal stability. In the application of cellulose conversion to TRS catalyzed by NADESs, the influencing factors including the types of NADESs, reaction temperature, reaction time, and FeCl36H2O addition amount on the TRS yield were studied. Among them, the L-Pro/EG/FeCl36H2O system showed the best performance with 85.6% cellulose conversion and 66.7%TRS yield at reaction time 120 min and reaction temperature 120 °C. The properties of NADESS can make the processes greener, which has great potential in industrial applications.

Natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESS) provide an attractive alternative for the "green" conversion of cellulose. In this work, series of amino acids based NADESS with FeCl36H2O as ligands catalyst were synthesized and characterized by in situ IR, FT-IR, 1H NMR and TG-DTA. NADESS showed great thermal stability. The efficient hydrolysis performance of cellulose in NADESs was inves-tigated under mild conditions. The influencing factors such as the type of NADESS, reaction temperature, reaction time, and FeCl36H2O addition on the TRS yield were studied. The optimized process conditions for hydrolyzing cellulose in L-Proline/ Ethylene glycol/FeCl36H2O were molar ratio 1: 2: 1, reaction time 120 min and tempera-ture 120 °C. The yield of total reducing sugar was 66.7%. The conversion mechanism was also investigated. © 2020 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. # 1. Introduction Concerns about fossil carbon depletion and global climate change have led to an increasing focus on biomass conversion to sustainably supply liquid fuels and valuable chemicals. Therefore, the search for renewable energy to replace fossil fuels has become a top priority. According to the forecast made by the US Department of Energy, the amount of liquid fuels consumed in the US from biofuels should increase 200% due to the Federal Renewable Fuels Standard, which requires 36 billion gallons of renewable fuel to be blended into transportation fuels by 2022 [1]. Recently, biomass conversion has become a research hotspot of many scholars at home and abroad, and different methods have been developed to convert biomass into fuels, chemicals and materials [2–5]. Biomass resources are the only renewable organic carbon resources in nature. Lignocellulose is the most abundant green renewable re-source and the main structural form of plants [6-9]. Lignocellulose con-sists of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin, with an annual production of about 170 billion tons, of which about 45% is cellulose [10-12]. The cellulose molecule contains a large amount of hydroxyl groups inside, and since hydrogen bonds are easily generated between the hydroxyl group and the hydroxyl group, a large number of hydrogen bonds exist inside and between the cellulose molecules, forming a strong hydrogen bond network structure [15–17]. Therefore, cellulose is extremely difficult to dissolve in water or other conventional organic solvents, which seriously affects the contact between the catalyst and cellulose molecules and becomes the biggest obstacle to cellulose conversion. In the past few decades, research on the conversion of cellulose has developed rapidly. Conversion of cellulose into various value-added chemicals and fuels, such as various alcohols [18], gluconic acid [19], 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) [20], lactic acid [21], pentanoic acid esters [22], 2,5-dimethylfuran [23], and levulinic acid [24], has been studied extensively in recent years. The catalytic oxidation of cellulose to total reducing sugars (TRS) is one of the most promising pathways. TRS is used as a fine chemical product, and it is widely used in the pharmaceutical, food and industrial industries. In recent decades, ionic liquids (ILs) have been thought of as suitable solvents instead of sulfuric acid for conversion owing to their unique properties, including negligible vapor pressure, high thermal stability, and good solvent power for different kinds of substances [25]. In 2018, Saliha Saher [26] synthesized a pyridinium-based ionic liquid [C4C₁Py] [Cl], which was used for the dissolution of cellulose, with a solubility of up to 28% at 110 °C, and continued in the presence of the metal salt https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molliq.2020.113282 0167-7322/© 2020 Elsevier B.V. However, high prices, poor toxicity and biodegradability limit the further application of traditional IL in the field of green chemistry. As an attractive alternative to ILs and conventional organic solvents, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged and have evolved signifi- cantly [27]. DESs are usually binary mixtures of hydrogen bond accep- tors (HBA) and hydrogen bond donors (HBD). At a certain molar ratio, the freezing point is lower than the melting point of the pure compound constituting DESs [28]. DESs have similar solvent properties to ILs such as the low-cost, good renewability and low toxicity [29]. Moreover, they are easy to prepare under mild conditions. In recent works, there are many DESs which have been prepared for cellulose conversion. In 2012, Francisco et al. [30]. obtained a variety of DES solvent systems using representative natural substances commonly found in nature such as amino acids, choline chloride, niacin, malic acid and lactic acid. It was found that most DES have weak cellulose conver- sion ability, and DES composed of proline and malic acid can also con- vert a certain amount of cellulose. In 2015, Procentese [31] synthesized glycerol/choline chloride (Gly/ChCl), urea/choline chloride (Urea/ChCl) and imidazole/choline chloride (Im/ChCl) DESs for corn core conversion. In this process, it was found that the DES promotes the saccharification conversion process by removing lignin and reduc- ing the crystallinity of the cellulose, and a total of 41 g of fermentable sugar (27 g of glucose and 14 g of xylose) can be recovered from 100 g of corn cob, accounting for 76% of the initial available reducing sugar. In 2016, Wahlstrom et al. [32] synthesized three choline chlo- rides: boric acid (5:2 M ratio), choline chloride: glycerol (molar ratio 1:1), and betaine: glycerol (molar ratio 1:1). The composition of the DES converted the wheat straw, and the stability of the wheat straw to TRS, and the yield after the residue hydrolysis were 33.0%, 20.0% and 19.0%, respectively. Overall, the conversion of cellulose in DESs is not ideal. Therefore, it is important to find efficient DESs with high con- version ability and selectivity to biomass. As a kind of Lewis acid, Iron (III) chloride hexahydrate (FeCl36H2O) is widely used as catalyst in chemical reactions such as esterification, condensation, etherification and oxidation. It has the advantages of high catalytic activity, reusability and low price [33]. FeCl36H2O catalyzed hydrolysis reaction conditions are mild, less corrosion to equipment, simple operation, short reaction cycle, low cost, and environmental protection. In this research, it was devoted to the synthesis of a novel series of amino acid based natural deep eutectic solvents (NADES) with FeCl36- H2O as ligands catalyst, and utilized to convert cellulose into the total re- ducing sugar. The physical properties of NADESs include freezing point, solvation parameters, pH, thermal stability and synthesis processes were investigated. The chemical properties of the NADESs such as ¹H NMR and FT-IR were also measured. The effects of different external fac- tors, such as different sorts of NADESs, temperature, time and FeCl36- H2O addition on cellulose conversion were studied. The conversion mechanism was also developed. ## 2. Experiments ### 2.1. Materials The cellulose was cotton linter pulp with a polymerization degree of 575.6 (Helon, China). The cotton linter pulp was cut into small pieces. After being dried at 100 °C for 12 h, the cellulose was prepared and used in the present study. N₂ (99.99%) was obtained from Beijing Haipu Gases Co., Ltd., Beijing, China. L-Proline, L-Lysine and L-Glutamic acid (99%) were purchased from Huayang Chemical Co., Ltd., Hebei, China. Iron(III) chloride hexahydrate (99%), Methanesulfonic acid (MSA) and p-Toluenesulfonic acid (TsOH) were obtained from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. Ethylene glycol and Glycerol (99%) was obtained from Tianjin Yongda Reagent Co., Ltd., Tianjin, China. All chemical reagents used in this work were of analytical grade purity and were used directly. 2.2. Synthesis of NADESS A series of natural deep eutectic solvents were synthesized accord-ing to the previously methods [34]. The amino acids (L-Proline, L-Lysine, L-Glutamic acid, etc.) were used as hydrogen bond acceptors, ethylene glycol, _p_-toluenesulfonic acid, Methanesulfonic acid, etc. were used as hydrogen bond donors, and FeCl₃·6H₂O as ligands were added to a 100 mL round bottom three-necked flask at a certain ratio. The mixture was then heated at a heating rate of 5 °C·h⁻¹ from room temperature to 100 °C under magnetic stirring. The container was also protected with nitrogen until a uniform, stable liquid formed. The sample was then placed in a forced air oven at 60 °C for 24 h, and the products were ob-tained (Fig. 1). 2.3. Conversion of cellulose in NADESs 5 g of prepared NADESs was added to a 100 mL round bottom flask, and then heated at a heating rate of 5 °C·h⁻¹ from room temperature to 140 °C under magnetic stirring. Then 1 g cellulose was added to the flask and allowed to react for 2 h at a set temperature from 90 °C to 140 °C. The reaction was terminated immediately by placing in an ice water bath. The cellulose conversion rate is calculated by measuring the change in mass before and after the reaction. After the reaction, the mixed solution was rapidly cooled, centrifuged and filtered. Ethanol was added to the solid residue as back extractant of cellulose. The insoluble cellulose solids were dried and weighed to calculate the conversion of cellulose [35]. PH The pH reflects the acidity of the solution, and it directly affects the conversion of cellulose. As shown in Fig. 6, the pH of NADESS was about 4-5 in the absence of FeCl3 · 6H2O, and it showed weak acidity. However, the acidity of the system increased to -1.8- -1.1 when FeCl3 · 6H2O was added. L-Lys/EG/FeCl3 · 6H2O was the most acidic sol- vent, but the yield of TRS was not the highest. It was possible that higher acidity would enhance certain side reactions, such as dehydration of glucose to 5-hydroxymethylfurfural. The acidity of L-Pro/EG/ FeCl3 · 6H2O was weaker than that of L-Lys/EG/FeCl3 · 6H2O, but the yield of TRS was the highest among these five systems. It could be con- cluded that proper acidity was favorable for increasing the TRS yield. 3.2.3. Solvation properties The Kamlet-Taft solvation model is often used to study the biomass conversion in liquid liquids or DESs. Solvation parameters include hydrogen bond acidity (α), hydrogen bond basicity (β), and polarizable effect (π*). The dipolar/polarizability is used to describe the non-specific part of the interaction between the solvent and the solute Van der Waals, such as dispersion, induction, and electrostatic interactions. Hydrogen bond basicity characterizes a compound's ability to give an electron pair as a hydrogen bond donor, and hydrogen bond acidic alpha indicates the compound's ability to accept an electron pair as a hydrogen bond acceptor. As shown in Table 3, L-Pro/EG NADESs differed greatly from the other four types of NADESs in solvation properties, which had higher α values (1.58), lower β values (0.53), smaller π* (0.73), and E_T (30) (68.27 kcal mol⁻¹). These solvation parameters insured that the hydrogen-bond interaction between L-Pro and EG was stronger than others. Besides, the L-Pro/EG NADESS solution had weaker polarizability and stronger polarity. It indicated that it would have a better ability to bind electrons, which was beneficial for the formation of hydrogen bonds between NADESs and cellulose, thereby promoting the conver-sion of cellulose. 3.2.4. Firstly, raw materials L-Proline, EG, and the ligands catalyst of FeCl36H2O reacted with each other to form O---HN and O---H---FeCl36H2O, and the L- Pro/EG/FeCl36H2O system was synthesized successfully. Secondly, 1,4- β glycoside bonds in cellulose were broken greenly under the strong acidity of L-Pro/EG/FeCl36H2O. Regeneration of NADESs In the regeneration of NADESs, the unreacted cellulose solid and the residual reducing sugars are all need to be removed. For the unreacted cellulose solid, it could be filtered when the reaction stopped. For the most part of NADESs, the sugar is insoluble in ethanol as studied [36–40], so the reducing sugars could be precipitated from ethylene glycol and glycerol with ethanol. Because the structure of the reducing sugars are similar to ethylene glycol and glycerol, the reducing sugars would react with amino acids (L-Proline) owing to the hydrogen bond between the two materials. The residual reducing sugars also need pu- rity from the amino acids (L-Proline). To solve this problem, the differ- ent polarity of L-Proline and the reducing sugars can be used [51]. L- Proline is a kind of non-polar amino acid, and the reducing sugars are polar substance. Therefore, the low-polarity butanone was introduced to "extract" L-Proline from the reducing sugars, and the high-purified NADES and catalyst mixture were regenerated. The reusability of NADESs was carried out, and the results showed that the TRS yield was 59.5% after eight recycles, which was slight decreased than that of the first run (66.7%) (Fig. S15). The NADESs has good catalytic stability in the hydrolysis of cellulose to TRS. ## 4. Conclusions In this work, a novel series of NADESS with FeCl36H2O as ligands catalyst were synthesized and applied in catalytic conversion of cellulose to TRS, which had great thermal stability. In the application of cellulose conversion to TRS catalyzed by NADESs, the influencing factors including the types of NADESs, reaction temperature, reaction time, and FeCl36H2O addition amount on the TRS yield were studied. Among them, the L-Pro/EG/FeCl36H2O system showed the best performance with 85.6% cellulose conversion and 66.7%TRS yield at reaction time 120 min and reaction temperature 120 °C. The properties of NADESS can make the processes greener, which has great potential in industrial applications. Natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESS) provide an attractive alternative for the "green" conversion of cellulose. In this work, series of amino acids based NADESS with FeCl36H2O as ligands catalyst were synthesized and characterized by in situ IR, FT-IR, 1H NMR and TG-DTA. NADESS showed great thermal stability. The efficient hydrolysis performance of cellulose in NADESs was inves-tigated under mild conditions. The influencing factors such as the type of NADESS, reaction temperature, reaction time, and FeCl36H2O addition on the TRS yield were studied. The optimized process conditions for hydrolyzing cellulose in L-Proline/ Ethylene glycol/FeCl36H2O were molar ratio 1: 2: 1, reaction time 120 min and tempera-ture 120 °C. The yield of total reducing sugar was 66.7%. The conversion mechanism was also investigated. © 2020 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. # 1. Introduction Concerns about fossil carbon depletion and global climate change have led to an increasing focus on biomass conversion to sustainably supply liquid fuels and valuable chemicals. Therefore, the search for renewable energy to replace fossil fuels has become a top priority. According to the forecast made by the US Department of Energy, the amount of liquid fuels consumed in the US from biofuels should increase 200% due to the Federal Renewable Fuels Standard, which requires 36 billion gallons of renewable fuel to be blended into transportation fuels by 2022 [1]. Recently, biomass conversion has become a research hotspot of many scholars at home and abroad, and different methods have been developed to convert biomass into fuels, chemicals and materials [2–5]. Biomass resources are the only renewable organic carbon resources in nature. Lignocellulose is the most abundant green renewable re-source and the main structural form of plants [6-9]. Lignocellulose con-sists of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin, with an annual production of about 170 billion tons, of which about 45% is cellulose [10-12]. The cellulose molecule contains a large amount of hydroxyl groups inside, and since hydrogen bonds are easily generated between the hydroxyl group and the hydroxyl group, a large number of hydrogen bonds exist inside and between the cellulose molecules, forming a strong hydrogen bond network structure [15–17]. Therefore, cellulose is extremely difficult to dissolve in water or other conventional organic solvents, which seriously affects the contact between the catalyst and cellulose molecules and becomes the biggest obstacle to cellulose conversion. In the past few decades, research on the conversion of cellulose has developed rapidly. Conversion of cellulose into various value-added chemicals and fuels, such as various alcohols [18], gluconic acid [19], 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) [20], lactic acid [21], pentanoic acid esters [22], 2,5-dimethylfuran [23], and levulinic acid [24], has been studied extensively in recent years. The catalytic oxidation of cellulose to total reducing sugars (TRS) is one of the most promising pathways. TRS is used as a fine chemical product, and it is widely used in the pharmaceutical, food and industrial industries. In recent decades, ionic liquids (ILs) have been thought of as suitable solvents instead of sulfuric acid for conversion owing to their unique properties, including negligible vapor pressure, high thermal stability, and good solvent power for different kinds of substances [25]. In 2018, Saliha Saher [26] synthesized a pyridinium-based ionic liquid [C4C₁Py] [Cl], which was used for the dissolution of cellulose, with a solubility of up to 28% at 110 °C, and continued in the presence of the metal salt https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molliq.2020.113282 0167-7322/© 2020 Elsevier B.V. However, high prices, poor toxicity and biodegradability limit the further application of traditional IL in the field of green chemistry. As an attractive alternative to ILs and conventional organic solvents, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged and have evolved signifi- cantly [27]. DESs are usually binary mixtures of hydrogen bond accep- tors (HBA) and hydrogen bond donors (HBD). At a certain molar ratio, the freezing point is lower than the melting point of the pure compound constituting DESs [28]. DESs have similar solvent properties to ILs such as the low-cost, good renewability and low toxicity [29]. Moreover, they are easy to prepare under mild conditions. In recent works, there are many DESs which have been prepared for cellulose conversion. In 2012, Francisco et al. [30]. obtained a variety of DES solvent systems using representative natural substances commonly found in nature such as amino acids, choline chloride, niacin, malic acid and lactic acid. It was found that most DES have weak cellulose conver- sion ability, and DES composed of proline and malic acid can also con- vert a certain amount of cellulose. In 2015, Procentese [31] synthesized glycerol/choline chloride (Gly/ChCl), urea/choline chloride (Urea/ChCl) and imidazole/choline chloride (Im/ChCl) DESs for corn core conversion. In this process, it was found that the DES promotes the saccharification conversion process by removing lignin and reduc- ing the crystallinity of the cellulose, and a total of 41 g of fermentable sugar (27 g of glucose and 14 g of xylose) can be recovered from 100 g of corn cob, accounting for 76% of the initial available reducing sugar. In 2016, Wahlstrom et al. [32] synthesized three choline chlo- rides: boric acid (5:2 M ratio), choline chloride: glycerol (molar ratio 1:1), and betaine: glycerol (molar ratio 1:1). The composition of the DES converted the wheat straw, and the stability of the wheat straw to TRS, and the yield after the residue hydrolysis were 33.0%, 20.0% and 19.0%, respectively. Overall, the conversion of cellulose in DESs is not ideal. Therefore, it is important to find efficient DESs with high con- version ability and selectivity to biomass. As a kind of Lewis acid, Iron (III) chloride hexahydrate (FeCl36H2O) is widely used as catalyst in chemical reactions such as esterification, condensation, etherification and oxidation. It has the advantages of high catalytic activity, reusability and low price [33]. FeCl36H2O catalyzed hydrolysis reaction conditions are mild, less corrosion to equipment, simple operation, short reaction cycle, low cost, and environmental protection. In this research, it was devoted to the synthesis of a novel series of amino acid based natural deep eutectic solvents (NADES) with FeCl36- H2O as ligands catalyst, and utilized to convert cellulose into the total re- ducing sugar. The physical properties of NADESs include freezing point, solvation parameters, pH, thermal stability and synthesis processes were investigated. The chemical properties of the NADESs such as ¹H NMR and FT-IR were also measured. The effects of different external fac- tors, such as different sorts of NADESs, temperature, time and FeCl36- H2O addition on cellulose conversion were studied. The conversion mechanism was also developed. ## 2. Experiments ### 2.1. Materials The cellulose was cotton linter pulp with a polymerization degree of 575.6 (Helon, China). The cotton linter pulp was cut into small pieces. After being dried at 100 °C for 12 h, the cellulose was prepared and used in the present study. N₂ (99.99%) was obtained from Beijing Haipu Gases Co., Ltd., Beijing, China. L-Proline, L-Lysine and L-Glutamic acid (99%) were purchased from Huayang Chemical Co., Ltd., Hebei, China. Iron(III) chloride hexahydrate (99%), Methanesulfonic acid (MSA) and p-Toluenesulfonic acid (TsOH) were obtained from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. Ethylene glycol and Glycerol (99%) was obtained from Tianjin Yongda Reagent Co., Ltd., Tianjin, China. All chemical reagents used in this work were of analytical grade purity and were used directly. 2.2. Synthesis of NADESS A series of natural deep eutectic solvents were synthesized accord-ing to the previously methods [34]. The amino acids (L-Proline, L-Lysine, L-Glutamic acid, etc.) were used as hydrogen bond acceptors, ethylene glycol, _p_-toluenesulfonic acid, Methanesulfonic acid, etc. were used as hydrogen bond donors, and FeCl₃·6H₂O as ligands were added to a 100 mL round bottom three-necked flask at a certain ratio. The mixture was then heated at a heating rate of 5 °C·h⁻¹ from room temperature to 100 °C under magnetic stirring. The container was also protected with nitrogen until a uniform, stable liquid formed. The sample was then placed in a forced air oven at 60 °C for 24 h, and the products were ob-tained (Fig. 1). 2.3. Conversion of cellulose in NADESs 5 g of prepared NADESs was added to a 100 mL round bottom flask, and then heated at a heating rate of 5 °C·h⁻¹ from room temperature to 140 °C under magnetic stirring. Then 1 g cellulose was added to the flask and allowed to react for 2 h at a set temperature from 90 °C to 140 °C. The reaction was terminated immediately by placing in an ice water bath. The cellulose conversion rate is calculated by measuring the change in mass before and after the reaction. After the reaction, the mixed solution was rapidly cooled, centrifuged and filtered. Ethanol was added to the solid residue as back extractant of cellulose. The insoluble cellulose solids were dried and weighed to calculate the conversion of cellulose [35]. PH The pH reflects the acidity of the solution, and it directly affects the conversion of cellulose. As shown in Fig. 6, the pH of NADESS was about 4-5 in the absence of FeCl3 · 6H2O, and it showed weak acidity. However, the acidity of the system increased to -1.8- -1.1 when FeCl3 · 6H2O was added. L-Lys/EG/FeCl3 · 6H2O was the most acidic sol- vent, but the yield of TRS was not the highest. It was possible that higher acidity would enhance certain side reactions, such as dehydration of glucose to 5-hydroxymethylfurfural. The acidity of L-Pro/EG/ FeCl3 · 6H2O was weaker than that of L-Lys/EG/FeCl3 · 6H2O, but the yield of TRS was the highest among these five systems. It could be con- cluded that proper acidity was favorable for increasing the TRS yield. 3.2.3. Solvation properties The Kamlet-Taft solvation model is often used to study the biomass conversion in liquid liquids or DESs. Solvation parameters include hydrogen bond acidity (α), hydrogen bond basicity (β), and polarizable effect (π*). The dipolar/polarizability is used to describe the non-specific part of the interaction between the solvent and the solute Van der Waals, such as dispersion, induction, and electrostatic interactions. Hydrogen bond basicity characterizes a compound's ability to give an electron pair as a hydrogen bond donor, and hydrogen bond acidic alpha indicates the compound's ability to accept an electron pair as a hydrogen bond acceptor. As shown in Table 3, L-Pro/EG NADESs differed greatly from the other four types of NADESs in solvation properties, which had higher α values (1.58), lower β values (0.53), smaller π* (0.73), and E_T (30) (68.27 kcal mol⁻¹). These solvation parameters insured that the hydrogen-bond interaction between L-Pro and EG was stronger than others. Besides, the L-Pro/EG NADESS solution had weaker polarizability and stronger polarity. It indicated that it would have a better ability to bind electrons, which was beneficial for the formation of hydrogen bonds between NADESs and cellulose, thereby promoting the conver-sion of cellulose. 3.2.4. Regeneration of NADESs In the regeneration of NADESs, the unreacted cellulose solid and the residual reducing sugars are all need to be removed. For the unreacted cellulose solid, it could be filtered when the reaction stopped. For the most part of NADESs, the sugar is insoluble in ethanol as studied [36–40], so the reducing sugars could be precipitated from ethylene glycol and glycerol with ethanol. Because the structure of the reducing sugars are similar to ethylene glycol and glycerol, the reducing sugars would react with amino acids (L-Proline) owing to the hydrogen bond between the two materials. The residual reducing sugars also need pu- rity from the amino acids (L-Proline). To solve this problem, the differ- ent polarity of L-Proline and the reducing sugars can be used [51]. L- Proline is a kind of non-polar amino acid, and the reducing sugars are polar substance. Therefore, the low-polarity butanone was introduced to "extract" L-Proline from the reducing sugars, and the high-purified NADES and catalyst mixture were regenerated. The reusability of NADESs was carried out, and the results showed that the TRS yield was 59.5% after eight recycles, which was slight decreased than that of the first run (66.7%) (Fig. S15). The NADESs has good catalytic stability in the hydrolysis of cellulose to TRS. ## 4. Conclusions In this work, a novel series of NADESS with FeCl36H2O as ligands catalyst were synthesized and applied in catalytic conversion of cellulose to TRS, which had great thermal stability. In the application of cellulose conversion to TRS catalyzed by NADESs, the influencing factors including the types of NADESs, reaction temperature, reaction time, and FeCl36H2O addition amount on the TRS yield were studied. Among them, the L-Pro/EG/FeCl36H2O system showed the best performance with 85.6% cellulose conversion and 66.7%TRS yield at reaction time 120 min and reaction temperature 120 °C. The properties of NADESS can make the processes greener, which has great potential in industrial applications.
